For young children, people with dementia, those with intellectual disability, or anyone who cannot work with the abstraction of a number, a faces scale showing a graded series of expressions or an observational scale scoring grimacing, guarding, vocalisation and restlessness captures the same information without requiring words. Behavioural observation is also the fallback for anyone whose report cannot be taken at face value. What separates useful pain assessment from a number written in a box is attention to character and trajectory, and to two specific patterns that carry disproportionate weight. The first is pain out of proportion to visible findings — severe, escalating pain over a limb or area that looks nearly normal is the classic early presentation of compartment syndrome, necrotising soft-tissue infection, and mesenteric ischaemia, three conditions in which tissue is dying faster than the surface reveals, and in all three the delay caused by trusting the unremarkable appearance is the usual reason outcomes are poor. The second is pain that is unrelieved by rest, position change or ordinary analgesia, or that wakes someone from sleep, which raises the threshold for investigation. Pain also has measurable physiological consequences rather than being merely unpleasant. Sympathetic nervous activation raises heart rate, blood pressure and oxygen demand, which is actively harmful in someone with heart disease. Chest or abdominal pain causes shallow, guarded breathing and suppresses coughing, so secretions pool at the lung bases and predispose to pneumonia after injury or surgery. Untreated severe pain also increases the likelihood of persistent chronic pain later. Adequate analgesia is therefore not a comfort layered on top of real treatment; it prevents a second, physiological problem arising from the first. One honest caveat: the historical worry that pain relief masks a surgical diagnosis has not held up well, though timing decisions remain a matter for clinical judgement.

sections.heading: Vital signs across the lifespan: pediatric and elderly considerations
sections.body: Adult normal ranges do not apply to children, and applying them is one of the more common and more dangerous errors in assessment. A newborn's heart rate normally runs 100 to 160 beats per minute and its respiratory rate 30 to 60 breaths per minute — figures that would signal serious illness in an adult. Both fall steadily with age: an infant of one year typically runs 100 to 150 beats and 25 to 40 breaths, a five-year-old around 80 to 120 beats and 20 to 30 breaths, and adult ranges are reached only in the early teens. The physiology behind this is worth knowing rather than memorising the table blindly. A small heart has a small stroke volume and limited ability to increase it, so a child compensates for any increased demand almost entirely by beating faster rather than harder; tachycardia is therefore the child's primary and earliest compensatory response, and it appears long before blood pressure changes. Children also have a much larger surface area relative to body mass and a higher metabolic rate, driving both faster baseline breathing and much faster heat loss. Blood pressure cuffs must be sized to the child's arm, and a systolic pressure below 90 that would alarm in an adult can be entirely normal in a young child. The critical and frequently misunderstood point is that a child's blood pressure is the last thing to fall. Children compensate so efficiently that pressure is often maintained until roughly a quarter of blood volume is lost, and when it does drop, collapse can follow within minutes. A normal blood pressure in a sick child is therefore reassuring about very little; heart rate, respiratory rate, capillary refill, skin colour and mental state are the signs that move first. Older adults present the mirror-image problem: their numbers can look alarming while they are well, or falsely reassuring while they deteriorate. Maximum achievable heart rate declines with age, approximated by 220 minus age, so an 80-year-old in serious trouble may be physiologically unable to mount the tachycardia a 25-year-old would show for the same insult. Beta-blockers, extremely common in this age group, blunt the heart-rate response still further and can hold a pulse near 70 through significant blood loss. Many older adults run a higher baseline blood pressure because of arterial stiffening, so a reading of 120 over 70 in someone whose usual pressure is 165 over 85 represents a substantial fall despite looking textbook-normal. Ageing also weakens the inflammatory response, so serious infection including sepsis frequently occurs with a normal or even low temperature; hypothermia in an older adult with infection carries a worse prognosis than fever. A normal temperature does not exclude serious infection in the old the way it more nearly does in the young, and new confusion is often the only early sign.

sections.heading: Trending vital signs and recognizing deterioration
sections.body: A single set of vital signs is a snapshot. A series taken over time is a trend line, and trends catch deterioration that snapshots systematically miss, because the body's compensatory mechanisms are specifically good at holding measured numbers inside normal ranges while the underlying problem worsens. Consider a patient recorded at 110 over 70 at one o'clock and the same 110 over 70 at four o'clock. Both readings sit comfortably in the normal band, and both would pass unremarked in isolation. If that person's usual pressure is 150 over 90, the reading represents a 40-point fall that has been present for hours — precisely the signature of early compensated shock, in which peripheral vessels clamp down hard enough to sustain central pressure even as circulating volume falls. This is why a person's own baseline matters more than the population range, and why asking what their blood pressure normally runs is one of the highest-yield questions available. Serial measurements — every 5 to 15 minutes in anyone unstable, and at minimum immediately before and after any intervention — reveal what no single careful reading can. One easily calculated early-warning number is the shock index: heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure. A healthy adult sits around 0.5 to 0.7; a pulse of 75 over a systolic of 120 gives 0.625. A shock index above roughly 0.9 to 1.0 flags significant blood loss or circulatory failure even when neither number alone looks dramatic. A pulse of 110 with a systolic of 100 gives 1.1: individually those are a mild tachycardia and a mildly low but arguably normal pressure, and together they are a clear warning, because the index captures a rising heart rate and a falling pressure working in the same direction rather than judging either in isolation. In trauma and post-partum haemorrhage the shock index has repeatedly outperformed either component alone at predicting the need for transfusion. Formal hospital early-warning scores apply the same logic more thoroughly, assigning points across respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, supplemental oxygen use, temperature, systolic pressure, heart rate and level of consciousness, then summing them; a total crossing a defined threshold triggers escalation. These systems work not because any single component is powerful but because several mildly abnormal values occurring together carry far more weight than one markedly abnormal value alone. Two practical cautions. First, a normal set of vital signs never overrides a person who looks or feels seriously unwell, and clinicians repeatedly find that a patient's own statement that something is badly wrong is a meaningful predictor. Second, record every reading with its timestamp in one place; a trend that exists only in memory is not a trend, and handing over a written sequence of numbers with times is worth more at the point of transfer than any verbal impression.

sections.heading: Assembling a Basic Assessment Kit
sections.body: A handful of inexpensive tools, most of them costing less than a restaurant meal, let you measure every vital sign covered here to a genuinely clinical standard, and understanding why each one earns its place matters more than owning it. The blood pressure cuff is the item where the choice actually matters. An automatic digital cuff is far easier for one person working alone and removes the skill of hearing Korotkoff sounds, but oscillometric devices estimate systolic and diastolic from the pattern of pressure oscillations using proprietary algorithms, and they become unreliable in atrial fibrillation, in shock, and at the extremes of pressure — exactly the situations where the number matters most. A manual cuff and stethoscope are cheaper, never need batteries, and remain accurate when the electronics give up, at the cost of practice. Whichever you choose, cuff size is not a detail: a cuff too narrow for the arm can over-read by 10 to 40 millimetres of mercury, which is the difference between reassurance and a diagnosis of hypertension, so match the cuff to the arm it will actually be used on and buy a large size if there is any doubt. A dual-head stethoscope in the fifteen to thirty dollar range is entirely adequate for blood pressure and for gross lung and heart sounds; the expensive models buy acoustic refinement that only matters once you can already distinguish what you are hearing. The pulse oximeter is the highest-value item per dollar in the kit, because falling oxygen saturation is often the first objective evidence of a deteriorating chest infection, and it is measurable before breathlessness looks obvious. Be aware that inexpensive units are least accurate at low saturations — precisely where accuracy matters — and that they read less reliably on darker skin, a bias documented in large studies, so treat readings near the 90 percent threshold as approximate and weight clinical appearance accordingly. A watch or phone with a visible seconds display is non-negotiable for counting rates honestly rather than estimating them. A penlight allows pupil size and reaction to be checked, and a logbook or a dedicated phone note is what turns isolated numbers into the trend that actually carries the information. A printed pain scale removes the temptation to reword the question differently each time, which is what destroys comparability between readings.
ingredients: A manual blood pressure cuff (sphygmomanometer) with a stethoscope, or an automatic digital cuff, from any pharmacy or medical-supply store — matched in size to the arm it'll be used on
A basic dual-head stethoscope ($15–30) for pulse, lung, and heart-sound checks
A fingertip pulse oximeter, an inexpensive clip-on device from any pharmacy, for oxygen saturation and pulse rate
A digital oral/axillary thermometer, or a no-contact forehead thermometer
A watch or phone with a visible seconds display, for timing pulse and respiratory counts
A small penlight, for pupil checks as part of a neurological exam
A notepad or phone note kept specifically for logging serial vital signs with timestamps
A printed 0–10 numeric pain-scale card, or a Wong-Baker FACES scale, freely available from public health sources

sections.heading: Step-by-step: a complete practice assessment
sections.body: The purpose of running a complete assessment on a healthy, willing volunteer is twofold, and the second reason is the more valuable one. The first is technique: counting a respiratory rate covertly, sizing and positioning a cuff correctly, and finding a radial pulse quickly are all manual skills that degrade without practice and cannot be learned during an emergency. The second is baseline. The single most useful piece of information when someone becomes unwell is what their numbers look like when they are well, because population ranges are wide and an individual's own values are narrow. Knowing that a family member normally runs 52 beats per minute and 145 over 85 turns two otherwise ambiguous readings into clear signals later. Order matters here for a practical reason. Count breathing first, before the person is aware of being observed, because respiratory rate is the only vital sign a subject can consciously alter without effort, and it is the one that most often gets estimated rather than measured. Take blood pressure after at least five minutes of quiet sitting: recent activity, caffeine within roughly 30 minutes, a full bladder, talking, an unsupported arm, or crossed legs each add measurable error, and together they can easily shift a reading by 20 points or more. Cross-check the oximeter's pulse figure against your manual count; a mismatch usually means a poor trace rather than a genuine deficit, and it is a useful reminder that the device reports what it can detect, not necessarily what the heart is doing. Repeat the whole sequence on a different day and at a different time, since temperature and heart rate follow a daily rhythm. Nothing measured here diagnoses anything, and an unexpected abnormal number in a well person is a reason for a routine appointment, not alarm.
steps: Have your subject sit quietly for at least 5 minutes before starting (activity, caffeine, and talking all skew the numbers) and record the time.
Count respiratory rate first, before they know you're doing it — watch chest rise for 30 seconds and double it, noting rhythm and effort.
Take a radial pulse for 30 seconds and double it, noting rhythm and strength alongside the rate.

Apply the blood pressure cuff to a bare upper arm at heart level, inflate about 30 mmHg above expected systolic, and slowly release, noting the systolic (first sound) and diastolic (sound disappears) — or use an automatic cuff.
Clip on a pulse oximeter, let it settle 15–30 seconds, and record both oxygen saturation and pulse rate, cross-checking against your manual pulse count.
Take a temperature reading, noting which method was used since normal ranges shift slightly between them.
Ask them to rate any current discomfort 0–10, and if there is any, run through OPQRST as practice.
Do a quick AVPU check: confirm they're oriented to person, place, and roughly the time, and note it as 'A, alert and oriented.'
Write every number down with the timestamp in one place, then repeat the whole sequence on a different day and compare what stayed the same and what shifted.

guides.title: Common Illnesses & Red Flags to Act On
guides.summary: A field guide to everyday illnesses — respiratory infections, gastrointestinal upset and dehydration, headaches, fever — and the specific 'red-flag' warning signs that mean stop-and-get-emergency-help now, including stroke (FAST), heart attack, sepsis and anaphylaxis. Educational and non-prescriptive; when in doubt, seek professional care.

sections.heading: How to think about symptoms and severity
sections.body: A symptom is what a person feels and reports — headache, nausea, dizziness — and a sign is what can be observed or measured by someone else, such as a fever, a rash, or a fast pulse. The distinction matters because symptoms alone are notoriously poor at separating trivial from dangerous illness, while a small number of specific signs separate them well. The great majority of illnesses are self-limiting: they resolve with rest, fluids and time regardless of what is done, which is why most home care is about comfort and monitoring rather than intervention. The genuinely useful skill is triage — sorting the minor from the dangerous — and three questions do most of the work. First, how fast did it come on? Symptoms that reach maximum intensity within seconds to minutes, such as the worst headache of someone's life, sudden one-sided weakness, or crushing chest pain, are far more concerning than an identical symptom that built gradually over days, because sudden onset implies a mechanical event like a rupture, a clot or a bleed rather than an inflammatory process. Second, what is the trajectory? An illness that is improving day by day, even slowly, is behaving normally; one that plateaus and then worsens after several days of improvement is the classic pattern of a secondary bacterial infection following a viral one. Third, are there red flags — specific danger signs that override any reassurance the overall picture provides. The general red flags applying across almost any illness are: difficulty breathing or breathlessness at rest, chest pain, confusion or any drop in alertness, a stiff neck accompanied by fever, a rash that does not fade when pressed, inability to keep any fluid down for more than several hours, severe unrelenting pain, fainting, and a person's own strong sense that something is seriously wrong. That last one is not sentimentality; the sense of impending doom is a recognised presenting feature of several catastrophic conditions and is worth taking at face value. In infants the signals differ: poor feeding, no wet nappies for eight hours or more, a bulging or noticeably sunken soft spot on the head, floppiness or unusual stiffness, a weak or high-pitched cry, and a baby who is difficult to rouse all warrant immediate assessment. Certain groups deteriorate faster and with subtler signs, so the threshold for seeking help should be lowered accordingly: infants and the very old, pregnant women, anyone with diabetes, anyone with a suppressed immune system from chemotherapy, steroids or immune-modifying drugs, and anyone without a functioning spleen. In these people a normal temperature and an unremarkable appearance provide considerably less reassurance than they would in a healthy adult, because the inflammatory response that produces the obvious signs is itself blunted.

sections.heading: Respiratory illness: colds, flu, and pneumonia
sections.body: The common cold is a viral infection of the upper airway, most often a rhinovirus, producing a runny or blocked nose, sore throat, sneezing, mild cough and either no fever or a low one. Symptoms peak around day two or three and settle over seven to ten days, though a dry cough can linger for two to three weeks after everything else has resolved, which is normal and not evidence of treatment failure. Influenza behaves differently and the distinction is usually clear at the bedside: onset is abrupt, often to the hour, with fever commonly between 38.5 and 40 degrees Celsius, prominent muscle aches, headache, a dry cough and a degree of exhaustion that keeps people in bed rather than merely uncomfortable. Both are viral, so antibiotics have no effect whatever on the illness itself, and taking them adds side effects and resistance without benefit. Care is supportive: rest, fluids, and paracetamol or ibuprofen for comfort. The danger lies in progression to the lower airway or a secondary bacterial infection on top of the viral one. Pneumonia, infection of the lung tissue itself, is suggested by a productive cough bringing up yellow, green or rust-coloured sputum, by a fever that returns or worsens after several days of improvement — a pattern often called double-worsening or double-sickening, and a genuinely useful discriminator — and by sharp chest pain that is worse on breathing in, called pleuritic pain, caused by inflamed pleural surfaces rubbing together. The single most important sign, however, is breathing: a respiratory rate above 20 to 24 per minute in a resting adult is the earliest reliable objective evidence that an upper respiratory illness has become something more, and it usually appears before the person feels obviously breathless. Red flags requiring urgent assessment are a respiratory rate above roughly 24 to 30 per minute, an oxygen saturation below 92 percent, blue discoloration of the lips or fingertips, new confusion, chest pain, coughing up blood, or an inability to complete a full sentence in one breath. Worked example: someone five days into what looked like an ordinary cold suddenly spikes a fever, is breathing 28 times a minute and reads 89 percent on a pulse oximeter. Each of those three findings alone would justify attention; together they indicate the illness has crossed from self-limiting into probable pneumonia, and the correct response is medical assessment rather than more bed rest. One honest caveat: sputum colour on its own is a weak indicator, since green sputum reflects enzymes released by white cells and occurs in viral illness too — it carries weight only alongside fever pattern and breathing rate. Counting breaths for a full minute while the person is unaware costs nothing and is far more informative than asking whether they feel short of breath, because people adapt to a gradual decline and consistently under-report it.

sections.heading: Gastrointestinal illness and dehydration
sections.body: Acute gastroenteritis, commonly called stomach flu although it is unrelated to influenza, is usually viral — norovirus and rotavirus dominate — and produces vomiting, watery diarrhoea, cramping and sometimes a low fever, typically resolving within one to three days. The illness itself is rarely the threat; dehydration from fluid loss is, and it remains a leading cause of death in young children worldwide for exactly this reason. Severe diarrhoea can strip several litres of fluid per day, and the very young, the very old and anyone in a hot climate reach dangerous depletion fastest because they have less reserve and less ability to signal thirst. Dehydration progresses through recognisable stages. Mild loss produces thirst and dark, scanty urine. Moderate loss adds a dry mouth, sunken eyes, absent tears in a crying child, skin that tents rather than springing back when pinched on the back of the hand, a fast pulse and lightheadedness on standing. Severe loss produces confusion, no urine passed for eight hours or more, a weak and rapid pulse, and cool, mottled skin — this is an emergency, because it means circulating volume has fallen far enough to compromise organ perfusion. Oral rehydration is the cornerstone of treatment and one of the most effective interventions in all of medicine. The mechanism is worth understanding: the gut has a sodium-glucose co-transporter that pulls sodium and glucose across the intestinal wall together, and water follows by osmosis. This transporter continues working even when the gut is inflamed and leaking, which is why a solution containing both salt and sugar is absorbed when plain water is not. A safe household preparation is one litre of clean or boiled-then-cooled water, six level teaspoons of sugar, roughly 30 grams, and half a level teaspoon of salt, roughly 2.5 grams. Do not exceed the salt: an over-salted solution is hypertonic and pulls water into the gut, worsening dehydration rather than correcting it, and this error has killed children. Give small volumes frequently — 5 to 10 millilitres every few minutes — even during ongoing vomiting, because small sips are often retained when a glassful is not. Red flags requiring medical assessment include blood in vomit or stool, black tarry stool indicating bleeding higher in the gut, severe or localised constant abdominal pain especially in the lower right, a rigid board-like abdomen, high fever, any sign of severe dehydration, or symptoms persisting beyond a few days. Avoid anti-diarrhoeal drugs such as loperamide when there is high fever or bloody stool, since slowing the bowel can retain an invasive bacterial infection and, in certain infections, precipitate serious complications. Urine output is the most practical home measure of adequate rehydration: someone passing pale urine every few hours is keeping pace with their losses, while eight hours of no urine at all indicates the kidneys are already conserving water aggressively.

sections.heading: Headaches and neurological red flags (stroke: FAST)
sections.body: Most headaches are benign and fall into two patterns. Tension-type headache is a dull, bilateral, band-like tightness, often described as pressure, commonly driven by stress, poor posture, sustained screen work, dehydration or missed meals. Migraine is typically throbbing, often one-sided, moderate to severe, worsened by routine activity, and accompanied by nausea and marked sensitivity to light and sound; roughly a quarter of sufferers experience an aura beforehand, most often visual — expanding zigzag lines or a blind spot developing over 5 to 30 minutes — caused by a slow wave of altered electrical activity spreading across the cortex. Both respond to rest, hydration, a dark quiet room and simple analgesia, though frequent use of painkillers more than about ten to fifteen days a month can itself cause a persistent medication-overuse headache, a common and easily missed trap. Certain features, however, mark a headache as potentially dangerous and warrant urgent assessment. A thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds suggests bleeding around the brain, most importantly subarachnoid haemorrhage, and the speed of onset matters more than the severity. So does the phrase worst headache of my life. Headache with fever and a stiff neck raises meningitis, particularly alongside a rash that does not fade under pressure. Headache with confusion, seizure, weakness, personality change or visual loss suggests a structural or infective cause. A genuinely new headache beginning after age 50, one following a head injury, one that is worse on lying flat or on waking, or one steadily worsening over days all justify assessment rather than observation. Stroke is the neurological emergency that must be recognised instantly, and the FAST check exists because it is memorable under stress. Face: ask them to smile and look for one side drooping. Arms: ask them to raise both arms and hold them; watch for one drifting downward. Speech: listen for slurred or garbled words, or an inability to repeat a simple sentence. Time: call emergency services immediately and note the exact time symptoms began, because eligibility for clot-dissolving treatment depends on that time and nobody else will know it. Stroke treatment is acutely time-dependent — an estimated 1.9 million neurons are lost per minute in a large-vessel stroke — so waiting to see whether it settles is the single most harmful response available. Other stroke presentations include sudden one-sided numbness, sudden severe dizziness with loss of balance, and sudden loss of vision in one eye. Symptoms that resolve within an hour still demand urgent assessment: a transient ischaemic attack carries a substantial risk of a full stroke within the following days, and the highest risk falls in the first 48 hours, which is precisely when people are most tempted to be reassured by the recovery. Never let someone with new neurological symptoms drive themselves anywhere.

sections.heading: Fever: what it is and how to manage it
sections.body: Fever is not a malfunction of temperature control but a deliberate upward shift of the body's thermostat, defined as a temperature of 38.0 degrees Celsius or 100.4 Fahrenheit and above. Infection triggers the release of signalling molecules that act on the hypothalamus to raise the set point, and the body then works to reach that new target — which is exactly why the onset of a fever feels cold, with shivering and goosebumps, despite the temperature rising. Understanding this explains several management points that otherwise seem arbitrary. Moderate fever appears to be genuinely useful: many bacteria and viruses replicate less efficiently at elevated temperature and several immune processes work faster, so suppressing every fever is not automatically beneficial. Crucially, the height of a fever correlates poorly with how dangerous the underlying illness is. A child with a temperature of 39.5 who is playing and drinking is far less concerning than one at 38.2 who is limp, unresponsive and refusing fluids. Appearance and behaviour carry more information than the number. Supportive management is rest, generous fluid intake — fever increases insensible fluid loss by roughly 10 percent per degree Celsius above normal — light clothing and a comfortable room. Antipyretic medicines such as paracetamol or ibuprofen improve comfort and are entirely reasonable for that purpose, but they are not obligatory if the person is comfortable, and reducing a number does not treat the cause. Do not sponge with cold water or alcohol: cold water triggers shivering, which generates heat and can raise core temperature, and alcohol is absorbed through skin, particularly in children, and can cause poisoning. Lukewarm water is acceptable if cooling is genuinely needed. Never give aspirin to a child or teenager with a viral illness because of the risk of Reye syndrome, a rare but frequently fatal swelling of the brain with liver failure. Red flags accompanying fever include a temperature at or above 40 degrees Celsius, 104 Fahrenheit, that does not respond to measures; fever with neck stiffness, severe headache or a rash that does not blanch under pressure; fever with breathing difficulty, chest pain or confusion; fever lasting beyond three to five days without improvement; fever in anyone immunosuppressed; and any fever at all in an infant under three months, which is a genuine emergency because such infants can harbour serious bacterial infection with almost no other signs. Febrile seizures occur in roughly two to five percent of young children, usually between six months and five years. They are frightening but generally benign: protect the child from injury, place them on their side, do not restrain them or put anything in the mouth, time the seizure, and seek assessment, urgently if it lasts beyond five minutes.

sections.heading: Chest pain, heart attack, and cardiac red flags
sections.body: Chest pain has many causes, most of them not dangerous — muscular strain reproducible by pressing on the chest wall, acid reflux producing burning behind the breastbone after meals or on lying flat, anxiety, and inflammation of the rib cartilage all present commonly — but heart attack must be considered first because it is the one where minutes change outcomes. A myocardial infarction occurs when a plaque in a coronary artery ruptures and a clot forms on it, cutting blood supply to a region of heart muscle; that muscle begins dying within roughly 20 to 30 minutes and the loss is largely irreversible after several hours, which is the entire reason for urgency. Classic warning features are pressure, squeezing, tightness or a heavy crushing sensation in the centre or left of the chest, lasting more than a few minutes or coming and going in waves; pain radiating to the left arm, jaw, neck, back or upper abdomen; and accompanying shortness of breath, cold sweat, nausea, lightheadedness or a strong sense of impending doom. Diaphoresis — sudden drenching sweat without exertion — is a particularly meaningful accompaniment. Presentations are frequently atypical, and this is where most missed diagnoses occur: women, older adults and people with diabetes, whose nerve damage can blunt pain perception, often present instead with unexplained fatigue, breathlessness, jaw or back discomfort, or symptoms indistinguishable from indigestion. Roughly a third of heart attacks occur without classic chest pain. For suspected heart attack, call emergency services immediately; that call is the single most important action and takes priority over everything else. Have the person sit and rest, loosen tight clothing, and keep them calm. If they are not allergic, have no bleeding disorder, and local guidance supports it, a single adult aspirin of 300 to 325 milligrams chewed rather than swallowed is absorbed faster and inhibits platelet clumping, which improves survival — but the call comes first, and driving someone to hospital yourself removes the possibility of treatment en route and of defibrillation if they arrest. Be prepared for cardiac arrest: if the person collapses and is not breathing normally, begin chest compressions in the centre of the chest at 100 to 120 per minute and 5 to 6 centimetres deep, allowing full recoil between compressions, and use an automated external defibrillator as soon as one is available, since survival falls by roughly 7 to 10 percent for every minute defibrillation is delayed. Reflux can often be distinguished by its burning character and response to antacids, but the honest position is that no bedside feature reliably excludes a cardiac cause, so treat uncertain chest pain as cardiac until proven otherwise. The cost of an unnecessary ambulance call is trivial; the cost of the opposite error is not, and people who die of heart attacks at home very often spent the preceding hour talking themselves out of calling.

sections.heading: Serious systemic red flags: sepsis and anaphylaxis
sections.body: Two life-threatening emergencies arise from otherwise ordinary triggers, and both are survivable when recognised quickly and frequently fatal when they are not. Sepsis is the body's dysregulated response to an infection, in which the inflammatory reaction that should be local becomes systemic and begins damaging the body's own organs. It can follow any infection — chest, urine, skin, gut, dental, or a wound so minor it was forgotten — and it kills roughly 11 million people a year worldwide, more than any single cancer. The mechanism explains the signs: widespread inflammation makes blood vessels leak and dilate, so blood pressure falls, tissues are starved of oxygen despite an adequate supply in the lungs, and organs begin to fail in sequence. Warning signs include slurred speech or new confusion, extreme shivering or severe muscle pain, passing no urine for a day, severe breathlessness, skin that is mottled, blotchy, bluish or unusually pale, and the person's own statement that they feel they might die — which is a recognised and meaningful feature, not melodrama. Supporting clues are a fever or, equally significantly, an abnormally low temperature, a heart rate above 90 to 100, fast breathing, and clammy skin. Sepsis is a time-critical emergency: mortality rises measurably for every hour that antibiotics and fluids are delayed, so seek care immediately and use the word sepsis explicitly, because it changes how urgently the concern is escalated. Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction that can kill within minutes, triggered most often by foods such as nuts, shellfish, eggs or milk, by insect stings, by medications, and by latex. It is distinguished from a milder allergic reaction by involving two or more body systems, or by a sudden drop in blood pressure after a known exposure. Typical involvement spans skin — hives, flushing, swelling of lips, tongue or throat — breathing, with wheeze, stridor, throat tightness or difficulty breathing, circulation, with dizziness, fainting or collapse, and gut, with vomiting and cramps. Treatment is adrenaline, also called epinephrine, injected into the outer mid-thigh without delay if an auto-injector is available and prescribed; it works within minutes by constricting blood vessels, opening airways and stabilising the cells releasing the reaction. Call emergency services immediately afterwards. Lie the person flat with legs raised if their blood pressure has dropped, or let them sit upright if breathing is the dominant problem, but do not stand them up suddenly — sudden upright posture after a pressure drop has been associated with fatal outcomes. A second dose may be needed after about five minutes without improvement. Antihistamines and asthma inhalers are not substitutes for adrenaline; they treat symptoms and do nothing for the collapse. Anyone treated for anaphylaxis needs observation even after recovering, because a delayed second wave can occur hours later without further exposure.

sections.heading: Skin infections and dangerous rashes
sections.body: Most skin redness is harmless, but a small set of patterns separates ordinary irritation from something that needs urgent attention, and the distinguishing features are learnable. Cellulitis is a bacterial infection of the skin and the tissue immediately beneath it, usually Streptococcus or Staphylococcus entering through a break that may be as trivial as an insect bite or a crack between the toes. It appears as red, warm, swollen and tender skin with a poorly defined, spreading border, developing over hours to days, most often on a lower leg. Because progression is what matters more than appearance at any single moment, marking the edge of the redness with a pen and noting the time is a genuinely useful bedside test: rechecking after four to six hours shows objectively whether it is advancing despite treatment, which no amount of staring at it will reveal. An abscess is a different problem with a different solution — a localised, fluctuant, exquisitely painful lump containing a pocket of pus, which generally requires drainage, since antibiotics penetrate a walled-off collection poorly. Far more dangerous is necrotising fasciitis, a rapidly spreading infection of the deep tissue planes that can advance several centimetres an hour and destroy tissue faster than the skin surface suggests. The cardinal clue is pain strikingly out of proportion to how unremarkable the skin looks, sometimes before any dramatic redness appears at all. Later signs include skin turning dusky purple, blistering or blackening, numbness in the area as the infection destroys cutaneous nerves, crackling under the skin from gas-forming organisms, and a person who is systemically far sicker — high fever, confusion, rapid heart rate, low blood pressure — than a simple skin problem would explain. This is a surgical emergency and delay is measured in outcomes, not inconvenience. A separate and equally important red flag is a rash that does not blanch. Press a clear drinking glass or a finger firmly against the rash: ordinary rashes are caused by dilated blood vessels and blanch, meaning the colour disappears under pressure and returns when released. If the discoloration remains visible under pressure, the rash is non-blanching, which indicates blood that has leaked out of vessels into the skin — small spots are called petechiae, larger patches purpura. In someone feverish, with severe headache or neck stiffness, a non-blanching rash is a hallmark of meningococcal sepsis and demands emergency care regardless of how well the person otherwise seems, because that infection can progress from mild symptoms to septic shock within hours. Two honest caveats: the rash appears late or not at all in a substantial minority of cases, so its absence proves nothing, and non-blanching spots confined to the face after violent vomiting or coughing are usually benign pressure effects.

sections.heading: Abdominal pain: the acute abdomen and its red flags
sections.body: Abdominal pain is genuinely hard to triage from the outside, because a dozen organs occupy a small space and the nerves supplying them report location poorly. Early pain from a hollow organ is carried by visceral nerves that are shared across wide regions, which is why it is felt vaguely near the midline and is hard to point to; only when inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum lining the abdominal wall, which has precise somatic innervation, does pain become sharp and localised. This shift from vague central discomfort to sharp, well-localised pain is itself a warning that the process has progressed. A few examination findings separate concerning from watch-and-wait reliably. Guarding is reflexive tensing of the abdominal muscles when pressed, distinct from simple tenderness, and its more serious form is rigidity, in which the wall is board-hard even at rest. Rebound tenderness — pain that is worse on releasing pressure than on applying it — reflects the same underlying irritation, since the wall springing back stretches an already inflamed peritoneum. Behaviour is diagnostic too: a person with peritonitis lies absolutely still because movement hurts, whereas someone with a kidney stone or biliary colic writhes and cannot find a comfortable position, and this contrast is often visible from the doorway. Location carries real diagnostic weight. Pain beginning vaguely around the navel and migrating over 12 to 24 hours to the right lower quadrant, maximal at McBurney's point about a third of the way from the hip bone to the navel, is classic appendicitis, which can perforate within roughly 48 to 72 hours and convert a contained infection into diffuse peritonitis. Right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal, radiating to the right shoulder blade, suggests gallbladder disease, the shoulder referral occurring because the diaphragm and that skin area share nerve roots. Severe pain boring through to the back in someone with gallstones or heavy alcohol use raises pancreatitis. Sudden tearing pain radiating to the back in an older adult with a pulsating abdominal mass suggests an aortic aneurysm and is immediately life-threatening. In any woman of childbearing age, sudden lower abdominal pain must be treated as a possible ectopic pregnancy until excluded, since rupture causes rapid internal bleeding. Treat as an emergency any abdominal pain that is severe, progressively worsening, accompanied by fever or persistent vomiting, associated with a rigid or exquisitely tender abdomen, or occurring with blood in vomit or stool. One important caveat: older adults and people on steroids frequently present with far less pain and less guarding than the severity of their underlying condition warrants, so a soft abdomen in those groups is considerably less reassuring than it appears. Withhold food and drink from anyone with severe abdominal pain until they have been assessed, since surgery may follow and a full stomach complicates anaesthesia.

sections.heading: Urinary tract infections and when they become an emergency
sections.body: A urinary tract infection usually begins in the bladder, where it produces burning on passing urine, a frequent and urgent need to go, passing only small volumes, cloudy or strong-smelling urine and mild discomfort low in the abdomen. At that stage it is unpleasant but rarely dangerous, and it is generally treated with a short course of oral antibiotics directed at the usual culprit, Escherichia coli, which ascends from its normal home in the bowel. Anatomy explains the epidemiology: the female urethra is roughly 4 centimetres long against about 20 in males, so bacteria have a far shorter journey, which is why uncomplicated bladder infection is common in women and structurally uncommon in men. The genuine red flag is infection climbing from the bladder up the ureters to the kidney, called pyelonephritis. It is marked by bladder symptoms plus fever, often high and with shaking chills known as rigors, flank pain in the back just below the ribs and typically on one side, nausea and vomiting, and a person who looks considerably sicker than a simple bladder infection would explain. A useful bedside check is costovertebral angle tenderness: place one hand flat over the angle where the lowest rib meets the spine and strike it once, firmly but gently, with the side of the other fist. Sharp pain reproduced there points toward kidney involvement, and comparing both sides makes an asymmetric result more convincing. Pyelonephritis matters because the kidney is richly supplied with blood, so an infected kidney is effectively a direct route into the bloodstream; untreated it can progress to bacteraemia and sepsis within days. It is treated more aggressively than a bladder infection, with a longer course and sometimes intravenous antibiotics and admission, particularly if vomiting prevents keeping tablets down, or if the person is pregnant, elderly, diabetic, has a single kidney or a stone, or shows any sign of sepsis. An obstructed, infected kidney — infection behind a blocking stone — is a urological emergency requiring drainage, because antibiotics alone cannot sterilise urine that has nowhere to go. Several situations warrant proper evaluation rather than repeated self-treatment: recurrent infections, visible blood in the urine, symptoms failing to improve within 48 hours of starting antibiotics, and any urinary infection in a man, which is far less common and more often linked to an enlarged prostate or a stone. One important caveat in older adults: confusion, falls or general decline may be the only presentation, with no urinary symptoms at all, while conversely bacteria are frequently present in the urine of older people without causing illness, so a positive urine test alone should not automatically be blamed for every symptom. Generous fluid intake supports treatment but does not replace it, and cranberry products have not been shown to treat an established infection.

sections.heading: A Home Illness-Monitoring Kit
sections.body: The purpose of a home monitoring kit is not to diagnose anything; it is to replace the unreliable impression that someone feels worse with objective numbers that can be compared over hours, because the single hardest judgement in home illness care is distinguishing feels bad from is actually deteriorating. Every item below exists to make one specific red flag measurable rather than guessed at. A digital thermometer earns its place through repetition rather than any single reading, since the shape of a fever curve carries far more information than its peak — a fever settling over three days is behaving normally, while one that resolves and then returns on day five is the classic pattern of a bacterial infection following a viral one. Buy one that reads in a few seconds; a slow thermometer simply will not be used often enough to build a curve. A fingertip pulse oximeter is arguably the highest-value item, because oxygen saturation falls measurably in a worsening chest infection before breathlessness becomes obvious to the person or to anyone watching, and it removes the guesswork from the single most important respiratory red flag. Understand its limits: it reads falsely low on cold fingers, through dark nail polish, and during movement, it reads less reliably on darker skin, and it reads falsely reassuring in carbon monoxide poisoning, so it must never be used to exclude that. A blood pressure cuff earns inclusion mainly for dehydration and deterioration, where a rising heart rate paired with a falling blood pressure is the objective signature of failing compensation long before someone looks shocked. A clear drinking glass is not a joke item — it is the entire equipment list for the blanching test that distinguishes an ordinary rash from bleeding under the skin. The permanent marker is equally serious: outlining the border of a spreading area of redness converts an unanswerable question into a simple comparison a few hours later. Oral rehydration packets are worth buying pre-made rather than mixed at home, because the salt concentration matters and an over-salted homemade solution actively worsens dehydration. Finally, the written symptom log is what makes all of the above useful, since a trend that exists only in memory is not a trend, and a timed sequence of numbers is the most valuable thing you can hand to a clinician.
ingredients: A digital thermometer (oral/axillary or no-contact forehead type, from any pharmacy) for tracking fever trends rather than a single reading
A fingertip pulse oximeter, to catch falling oxygen saturation in respiratory illness before breathing looks obviously labored
A basic blood pressure cuff, useful for tracking dehydration (a falling blood pressure with a rising heart rate on standing) and general deterioration
A clear drinking glass, for the 'glass test' on a suspicious rash
A permanent marker, for outlining the edge of a spreading area of redness so you can objectively see whether it's advancing
An oral rehydration solution packet, or the ingredients to make one (clean water, sugar, and salt in a standard ratio — pre-made packets are widely sold at any pharmacy or grocery store)
A written symptom log (paper or phone note) with columns for time, temperature, heart rate, and a short symptom description

sections.heading: Step-by-step: building your own symptom-triage habit
sections.body: The reason to rehearse these checks during a minor illness, or on a healthy volunteer, is that none of them are difficult but all of them are hard to perform correctly for the first time under stress. Recognition is a skill that degrades sharply with adrenaline, and the specific failure mode in an emergency is not forgetting what a red flag is — it is failing to think of checking at all, because attention narrows onto whatever is most dramatic. Practising the sequence when the stakes are zero builds the habit of looking, which is the part that actually transfers. Two of these deserve particular emphasis. Rehearsing the FAST stroke check on someone healthy takes fifteen seconds and is worth doing precisely because a real stroke often does not look like the dramatic collapse people expect; it can look like someone who seems slightly confused, or whose smile is subtly uneven, and the difference between recognising that immediately and waiting an hour to see is measured in permanent disability. Similarly, doing the glass test on an ordinary rash teaches you what blanching looks like, so that a non-blanching rash registers as obviously different rather than merely ambiguous. Keep expectations honest about what this practice does and does not achieve. It builds pattern recognition for the specific findings described here; it does not produce diagnostic ability, and it should never delay seeking help. If a check is ambiguous, treat it as positive. The written cheat sheet matters more than it sounds, because writing it in your own words forces you to actually understand each item rather than recognise it, and because a piece of paper on a fridge works when memory does not.
steps: The next time someone has a fever, take and log their temperature every 4–6 hours rather than once, and note whether it's trending up, flat, or down over the day.

Practice the FAST stroke check as a dry run on a healthy family member: ask them to smile (Face), raise both arms (Arms), and repeat a sentence (Speech), so the sequence is automatic if you ever need it for real.

If anyone has a rash, do the glass test: press a clear glass firmly against it and watch whether the color disappears (blanching, reassuring) or stays visible (non-blanching, a red flag if paired with fever).
Practice checking for abdominal guarding on a healthy volunteer: press gently on each of the four abdominal quadrants and feel for reflexive muscle tensing.
Time how long it takes a family member to rehydrate after exercise using an oral rehydration mix versus plain water, to build a feel for how GI fluid losses differ from ordinary thirst.
Write a one-page red-flags cheat sheet in your own words summarizing FAST, sepsis, anaphylaxis, and chest-pain warning signs, and put it somewhere visible.
Review your household's known allergies and physically locate any epinephrine auto-injector now, before an emergency, so no one is searching for it during one.

guides.title: Deep Wound Care, Bleeding Control & Infection
guides.summary: A practical, step-by-step reference for controlling bleeding (direct pressure, wound packing, tourniquets), cleaning and irrigating wounds, deciding on closure and dressings, and recognizing and managing wound infection and tetanus risk — with specific pressures, volumes, times and a worked example. Educational only; deep or serious wounds need professional care.

sections.heading: Wound types and the four phases of healing
sections.body:
A wound is any break in the continuity of the skin or the tissue beneath it, and the sensible starting point is that different geometries of injury fail in different ways. An abrasion is a scrape that strips the epidermis and part of the dermis across a broad area; it bleeds little, hurts a great deal because so many nerve endings are exposed, and its main danger is grit ground into the surface. A laceration is a tear with ragged, irregular edges, typically produced when blunt force splits skin over an underlying bone. An incision is a clean-edged cut from a blade or glass, which heals well precisely because the edges meet. A puncture is deep and narrow — a nail, a fang, a fishhook — and is the most treacherous common wound, because contamination is carried deep, the narrow track drains poorly, and the small opening on the surface tells you almost nothing about what is happening several centimetres down. An avulsion tears a flap or a piece of tissue away, and an amputation removes a part entirely.

Whatever the geometry, repair runs through four overlapping phases, and nearly every sensible care decision follows from knowing which phase a wound is in. Hemostasis begins within seconds: injured vessels constrict, platelets stick to exposed collagen and clump together, and the clotting cascade converts fibrinogen into a fibrin mesh that traps blood cells into a stable clot, usually within about three to ten minutes in someone with normal clotting. Inflammation follows and dominates roughly day zero to day three: vessels become leaky, neutrophils and then macrophages arrive to digest bacteria and dead tissue, and the wound turns red, warm, swollen and tender. That is normal and expected. It is emphatically not proof of infection, and mistaking it for infection is the single most common early error.

Proliferation runs from roughly day three to day twenty-one. Fibroblasts lay down collagen, new capillaries sprout into the wound bed, the surface fills with beefy pink granulation tissue, and epithelial cells crawl inward from the wound margins to resurface it. A moist surface lets those cells migrate across; a dry, hard scab forces them to tunnel underneath, which is slower. Remodeling then continues from about three weeks out to one or two years, as the hastily deposited type III collagen is gradually replaced by stronger type I collagen aligned along lines of tension. Even fully mature scar reaches only about eighty per cent of the surrounding skin's tensile strength, and never regrows hair follicles or sweat glands.

Good care simply protects that sequence: stop the bleeding, remove contamination, keep the wound clean and appropriately moist, and watch for infection. Anything that starves the wound of blood, oxygen or building blocks slows it down — peripheral vascular disease, diabetes, smoking, corticosteroid use, advanced age, and inadequate protein, vitamin C or zinc.

sections.heading: Bleeding control: direct pressure first
sections.body:
Severe bleeding kills faster than infection, faster than pain, and faster than almost anything else you will meet in a first-aid situation, so it outranks cleaning, splinting and reassurance absolutely. Three patterns are worth telling apart at a glance. Capillary bleeding oozes slowly from a broad raw surface and generally stops on its own. Venous bleeding is a steady, welling flow of dark red blood under low pressure, which can still be substantial from a large vein. Arterial bleeding is bright red because it is fully oxygenated, and it spurts in time with the pulse because it is driven by systolic pressure; a partly divided artery can empty a person in a few minutes.

The intervention that solves the overwhelming majority of bleeding is unglamorous: firm, sustained, correctly located direct pressure. Put on gloves if you have them, because blood-borne infection is a genuine risk to the rescuer, and a plastic bag over the hand is a workable substitute. Place a clean cloth or gauze pad directly onto the bleeding point rather than vaguely onto the limb, and press hard with the heel of the hand or with fingertips concentrated over the source. Pressure works because it mechanically opposes the arterial pressure pushing blood out and holds the torn vessel walls close enough together for platelets and fibrin to bridge the gap.

Hold continuously for at least ten minutes by a clock, and do not lift the dressing to check. Every peek shears off the fragile forming clot and restarts the ten minutes. If blood soaks through, leave the original dressing where it is and add further pads on top while still pressing; pulling a soaked dressing off strips the clot with it. Elevating the injured limb above heart level lowers local hydrostatic pressure and helps modestly, but only where no fracture is suspected. Once bleeding stops, apply a pressure dressing — a pad plus a firmly wrapped bandage — that is snug but never tourniquet-tight. Then check circulation beyond it: the skin should stay warm and pink, and a pinched fingernail or toenail should regain colour in under two seconds. If it does not, the dressing is too tight and must be loosened.

Judging blood loss matters, because the body conceals it well. An average adult holds roughly five litres. Losing up to about 750 millilitres, some fifteen per cent, produces little more than mild anxiety and a slightly fast pulse. Between roughly 750 and 1,500 millilitres the pulse rises above 100, the skin turns cool and pale as peripheral vessels clamp down, and the person becomes thirsty. Beyond about 1,500 to 2,000 millilitres, blood pressure falls, breathing becomes rapid and shallow, and confusion sets in — decompensated shock, which deteriorates quickly. Lay the person flat, keep them warm because cold blood clots poorly, give nothing by mouth, and get emergency help moving immediately.

sections.heading: Wound packing and tourniquets for life-threatening bleeding
sections.body:
When firm direct pressure on the surface fails to control severe bleeding, the reason is almost always that the torn vessel sits deep inside a cavity and your hand is compressing skin above it rather than the vessel itself. Two escalations address that. Both are for genuinely life-threatening bleeding, not for a cut that merely looks alarming.

Wound packing solves the depth problem directly. It applies to deep wounds of the limbs, the groin, the armpit and the junctional areas a tourniquet cannot reach, and it must never be used on the chest, the abdomen, the neck or the skull, where packing can do serious harm and the bleeding source is not accessible in any case. Take a roll of gauze — plain gauze works, while hemostatic gauze impregnated with kaolin or chitosan accelerates clotting and is better if available — locate the bleeding source with a gloved finger, and feed the gauze into the wound tightly, packing hard right down onto the bleeding point and then filling the entire cavity so nothing can shift. Tightness is the whole point; a loosely stuffed wound simply fills with blood around the gauze. Then hold hard direct pressure over the packed wound for at least three minutes, ideally ten, before dressing firmly over it. The packing transmits your hand pressure to the depth where the vessel is torn and gives the forming clot a physical scaffold.

A tourniquet is for life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that pressure and packing cannot stop: a partial amputation, a mangled limb, an arterial spurt you cannot reach. A commercial windlass tourniquet is far more reliable than anything improvised. If improvising, use a strip of strong cloth at least five centimetres wide, never a cord, wire, bootlace or belt buckle, which cut into tissue and cannot generate even pressure, plus a rigid stick as a windlass and something to lock it once tight. Place it roughly five to seven centimetres above the wound, between the wound and the heart, and never directly over a joint; if the wound is at or near a joint, go above it. In a chaotic scene, high and tight on the limb is acceptable and can be repositioned later.

Tighten until bright red bleeding stops completely and the pulse beyond it disappears. It will hurt severely, which is expected and is not a reason to ease off. A half-tightened tourniquet is worse than none at all, because it occludes low-pressure veins while arteries keep filling the limb, increasing total blood loss. Write the exact time of application on the tourniquet or on the person's forehead; the receiving hospital needs it to judge reperfusion risk. Do not loosen or remove it — that decision belongs to clinicians with resuscitation immediately available. Up to roughly two hours is well tolerated by a limb, and the limb is always subordinate to the life.

sections.heading: Cleaning and irrigation: removing contamination
sections.body:
Once bleeding is controlled, the dominant determinant of whether a wound becomes infected is how much bacteria and foreign material remains inside it. Infection is largely a numbers game: intact skin resists contamination easily, but a bacterial load above roughly one hundred thousand organisms per gram of tissue is the classic threshold beyond which most wounds become clinically infected, and dead tissue, soil and retained clot lower that threshold sharply. Crucially, what removes bacteria is mechanical flushing — the volume and pressure of clean fluid — rather than the antiseptic properties of whatever you flush with.

Wash your hands and put on gloves first. Then irrigate with a large volume of clean fluid at a modest, controlled pressure. Sterile saline is ideal, but a substantial body of evidence shows potable tap water performs equally well for routine wounds and is far more likely to be available; where the supply is doubtful, boil it and let it cool. A reasonable working figure is 50 to 100 millilitres of fluid per centimetre of wound length, and considerably more for anything visibly dirty. A five-centimetre gash contaminated with soil deserves half a litre or more, and the honest endpoint is not a number but run-off that comes out clear.

Pressure matters as much as volume. Around five to eight pounds per square inch dislodges adherent bacteria and particles without driving them deeper or damaging tissue. A 20 to 60 millilitre syringe fitted with an 18-gauge catheter tip or a splash shield produces approximately that, and so does a clean plastic bottle or bag with a small hole punched in it and squeezed firmly. Pouring water gently from a jug is far too weak to clean anything below the surface; a pressure washer or a hard hose jet is far too strong, forcing contamination along tissue planes and stripping viable tissue.

Remove visible grit, gravel, glass or splinters with clean or flame-sterilised tweezers under good light. Road grit left in a facial wound tattoos permanently and is worth real effort to pick out within the first day. A large impaled object — a knife, a spike, a length of reinforcing bar — is left exactly where it is and stabilised with bulky padding on both sides, because it may be the only thing compressing a divided vessel; removal belongs in an operating theatre. Scrub the intact skin around the wound, not the wound bed itself.

What you must not pour into an open wound matters just as much. Hydrogen peroxide, full-strength povidone-iodine, alcohol and strong detergents are cytotoxic: they kill fibroblasts and migrating epithelial cells along with the bacteria, and their brief antiseptic advantage is outweighed by delayed closure. Reserve antiseptics for the intact perimeter. Butter, flour, dirt, cobwebs, engine grease and chewing tobacco are folk remedies that reliably introduce contamination. Clean water, in quantity, at moderate pressure, is the workhorse.

sections.heading: Closure decisions and dressings
sections.body:
Closing a wound is not automatically better than leaving it open, because a closed wound is a sealed compartment: whatever bacteria are inside stay inside, warm, moist and undisturbed. Closure therefore suits wounds that are clean, fresh and well perfused, and the decision hinges on contamination, elapsed time, blood supply and mechanism.

Elapsed time matters because bacteria multiply on a logarithmic curve. The traditional golden period is roughly six hours for the trunk and limbs, extending to around twelve to twenty-four hours on the face and scalp, whose blood supply is so rich that infection is markedly less likely. A clean, straight-edged cut that gapes open when the limb is relaxed can reasonably be approximated within that window. Small gaping wounds can often be closed without stitches: adhesive closure strips laid perpendicular across the wound with a few millimetres of gap between them so fluid can still drain, or a cyanoacrylate skin adhesive run along the top of edges held together by hand — never inside the wound, where it behaves as a foreign body. Both work only after thorough cleaning, and only where skin tension is low.

Certain wounds should be deliberately left open to heal from the base upward, or referred onward. Puncture wounds, any animal or human bite, wounds older than roughly a day, visibly dirty or already inflamed wounds, and crush injuries in which a rim of tissue will die over the following days all fall into this group; closing them reliably creates an abscess. Wounds needing professional closure include those deep enough to expose yellow fat, muscle or tendon; gaping wounds longer than one to two centimetres; wounds crossing a joint or on the face, where alignment determines the final appearance; wounds that keep bleeding despite pressure; and any wound accompanied by numbness, weakness or an inability to move a finger normally, which suggests nerve or tendon division and needs surgical exploration rather than a dressing.

Dressings do considerably more than cover. Decades of evidence support moist wound healing: a wound kept slightly moist re-epithelialises roughly twice as fast as one allowed to dry into a hard scab, because epithelial cells migrate readily across a moist bed but must burrow beneath a dry crust. In practice, apply a thin film of plain white petrolatum, or an antibiotic ointment if you have one and the person is not sensitised to it, since neomycin causes contact dermatitis in a noticeable minority. Cover with a non-adherent sterile pad large enough to overlap intact skin, and secure with tape or a bandage that does not constrict. Change it daily, or sooner if it becomes wet, soiled or soaked through, cleaning gently at each change and using the opportunity to inspect for early infection. Keep the dressing dry between changes. A clean, adherent scab is a biological dressing and should not be picked off. For large, deep, heavily contaminated or awkwardly located wounds, transporting the person to care beats improvising closure at home.

sections.heading: Recognizing and managing infection
sections.body:
Distinguishing normal inflammation from infection is the most useful single skill in wound care, and the discriminator is the time course rather than any individual sign. Redness, warmth, swelling and tenderness during the first forty-eight hours are the expected inflammatory response, white cells arriving to clear debris. Infection announces itself by worsening after day two or three instead of steadily improving. A wound that was getting better and then becomes more painful is suspicious until proven otherwise.

The specific features to watch for are redness spreading outward beyond the wound margin, pain that increases rather than fades, escalating swelling and heat, and discharge that is thick, cloudy, yellow-green or foul-smelling. Thin, clear or slightly blood-tinged fluid in the first days is serous exudate and entirely normal. The most useful field technique is to draw around the outer edge of the redness with a pen and write the time beside it. Twelve hours later, whether that line sits inside or outside the current redness converts a subjective impression into an objective observation, and it is precisely the piece of information a clinician will want. Systemic signs — a temperature above about 38 degrees Celsius, chills, malaise, loss of appetite, a rising resting pulse — mean the infection is no longer purely local.

A red streak running from the wound toward the trunk is lymphangitis, bacteria tracking up lymphatic channels, often with tender swollen nodes in the groin or armpit. That warrants urgent assessment the same day. So does any wound infection in someone with diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, an immune-suppressing illness or medication, or no functioning spleen; in these groups infection progresses faster and more quietly, and the usual warning signs are blunted.

Early, mild, strictly local infection is managed by cleaning the wound, keeping it covered, applying warm compresses for twenty minutes several times daily to improve local blood flow, elevating the part to reduce swelling, and observing closely against a marked outline. If a tender, fluctuant lump has formed, that is an abscess, and antibiotics alone will not cure it; abscesses need drainage, which is a procedure rather than a home remedy. Do not start leftover antibiotics from a previous illness. The wrong drug, at the wrong dose, for the wrong duration selects for resistant organisms, can partially suppress an infection into a smouldering deep one, and strips away the diagnostic clarity a clinician needs.

The one true emergency is necrotising soft-tissue infection. Its hallmark is pain grossly out of proportion to what the wound looks like, together with rapidly advancing swelling, skin that turns dusky, mottled, blistered or numb, sometimes crackling under the fingers, and a person who looks systemically unwell and frightened. It can advance several centimetres an hour. This is a surgical emergency measured in hours, not days; summon help immediately rather than waiting to see whether it settles.

sections.heading: Tetanus, special wounds, and a worked example
sections.body:
Tetanus is caused not by rust but by Clostridium tetani, an anaerobic spore-forming bacterium living in soil, dust and animal faeces. Its spores germinate only in low-oxygen tissue, which is why deep punctures, crush injuries and wounds containing dead tissue are the classic settings, and why a rusty nail is dangerous for its geometry and soil contamination rather than for its rust. The organism releases tetanospasmin, a toxin that travels up nerves and blocks the inhibitory signals that normally let muscle relax, producing sustained spasm: lockjaw, arching of the back, and eventually spasm of the breathing muscles. Mortality remains substantial even with intensive care, and nothing reverses toxin already bound to nerve.

Prevention is therefore entirely a matter of immunisation. A tetanus-containing booster is recommended every ten years for routine protection, and within five years for a wound that is dirty, deep, punctured or soil-contaminated. If the last dose is unknown or overdue after such a wound, seek advice promptly; for a high-risk wound in someone incompletely immunised, tetanus immunoglobulin may be given alongside the vaccine to provide immediate passive protection while the vaccine takes effect.

Bites form their own category. Animal and human mouths carry dense mixed flora — Pasteurella from cats and dogs, Eikenella from humans — and cat bites are the worst of all, because needle-sharp teeth inoculate deeply through a tiny hole that seals over within hours. Bites are irrigated copiously and generally not closed. Any bite from a mammal where rabies circulates, or from a bat under any circumstances, is a medical emergency: wash for a full fifteen minutes with soap and running water, which by itself substantially reduces risk, then seek post-exposure prophylaxis without delay, because rabies is essentially always fatal once symptoms appear. Human bites over the knuckles, typically from a punch landing on teeth, seed the joint space and infect notoriously.

Burns need cool running water, not iced water, for about twenty minutes, and this remains worth doing up to roughly three hours after the injury, followed by loose covering with clean non-stick material or cling film laid on rather than wrapped tightly. Do not apply butter, toothpaste or ice, and do not deliberately burst blisters.

Consider a worked example. A gardener tears open a forearm on a rusty fence: a five-centimetre gaping laceration, visibly dirty, bleeding steadily. The correct sequence is direct pressure for ten uninterrupted minutes to stop the bleeding first; then copious irrigation with clean water, at least 250 to 500 millilitres and more if grit persists, continuing until run-off is clear; then a closure decision. Because it gapes, exceeds two centimetres, and was contaminated with soil and rust, it warrants professional closure and a review of tetanus status rather than home closure strips, which would seal contamination inside. Then a clean non-stick dressing for transport, and daily inspection over the following week for spreading redness, pus, red streaking or fever.

sections.heading: Burns: classification and specific wound care
sections.body:
Burns form their own wound category because the injury is thermal rather than mechanical, arrives as a gradient of damage running from the surface downward, and continues to evolve for one to three days after the event — a burn that looks superficial on the first evening can declare itself deeper by the third day. Depth determines both appearance and danger. A superficial burn, formerly called first-degree, involves only the epidermis: red, dry, painful, blanching white under a pressed finger, no blisters, healed in about a week without scarring. Ordinary sunburn is the archetype. A partial-thickness burn extends into the dermis and blisters, because fluid leaks from damaged capillaries and lifts the epidermis away from the layer below. It looks wet, pink or mottled red, and it is intensely painful precisely because dermal nerve endings are injured yet still functioning. Superficial partial-thickness burns heal in one to three weeks with little scarring; deep partial-thickness burns, whose surface is drier and blotchier with reduced sensation, heal slowly and usually scar. A full-thickness burn destroys the entire dermis and may extend into fat, muscle or bone, appearing white, waxy, leathery or charred, refusing to blanch, and often painless at its centre because the nerve endings there are destroyed. A burn that looks dreadful and does not hurt in the middle is worse, not better.

Estimating size drives every decision about fluid replacement and transfer. The Rule of Nines assigns roughly nine per cent of adult body surface to each arm, eighteen per cent to each leg, eighteen per cent each to the front and the back of the trunk, nine per cent to the head and one per cent to the genitals. For scattered or irregular burns, the burned person's own palm including the fingers approximates one per cent of their body surface — use their hand, not yours. Children have proportionally larger heads and smaller legs, so the adult rule overestimates limb burns in a small child.

Any full-thickness burn, any burn covering more than about ten per cent of body surface, and any burn involving the face, hands, feet, genitals, perineum or a major joint warrants professional evaluation. So does any circumferential burn encircling a limb or the chest, where tightening dead skin can strangle circulation or restrict breathing as swelling develops. Suspect inhalation injury where there is soot around the nose or mouth, singed nasal hair, hoarseness, or a burn sustained in an enclosed space; that airway can swell shut over hours.

Immediate care is cool running water, around fifteen degrees Celsius, for ten to twenty minutes, which genuinely limits the eventual depth of tissue damage when started promptly, followed by a loose non-adherent sterile dressing or clean cling film. Never apply ice directly; it adds a freezing injury on top of the burn. Remove rings and watches early, before swelling makes it impossible. Intact blisters are usually left alone as a sterile biological dressing, while large, tense or already-broken blisters are better deroofed and dressed than left as a flap trapping bacteria.

sections.heading: Chronic wounds and pressure injuries
sections.body:
Most wounds march through the ordinary four-phase repair sequence and close. A wound that stalls — conventionally defined as failing to progress meaningfully over four to six weeks — is chronic, and it is stalled for a reason: it is stuck in the inflammatory phase by continuing pressure, poor arterial inflow, poor venous outflow, persistent infection, or repeated trauma. Naming that cause is the treatment, because no dressing heals a wound whose underlying insult continues unchecked.

Pressure injuries, still widely called bedsores, illustrate the mechanism most clearly. The capillaries perfusing skin operate at roughly 32 millimetres of mercury. Lying on a firm surface generates interface pressures over a bony prominence that comfortably exceed that figure, so blood flow to the patch simply stops. Muscle is more metabolically demanding than skin and dies first, which is why the visible surface wound is often the small tip of a much larger cone of dead tissue underneath: the injury develops from the inside outward, and by the time skin breaks the damage is well established. Classic sites are the sacrum, the heels, the greater trochanters at the hips, the ischial tuberosities in a seated person, the elbows, and the back of the head in infants. Staging runs from Stage 1, intact skin with persistent redness that does not blanch under pressure, through Stage 2, a partial-thickness loss such as a shallow open sore or an intact blister, to Stage 3, full-thickness loss extending into fat, and Stage 4, exposing muscle, tendon or bone. A dark purple or maroon patch of intact skin is a deep tissue injury and frequently heralds a Stage 3 or 4 wound emerging over the following days.

Prevention is almost entirely mechanical and entirely achievable. Reposition an immobile person at least every two hours, and prompt a seated person to shift weight every fifteen minutes. Offload heels completely by floating them on a pillow rather than resting them on the mattress. Use pressure-redistributing foam or alternating-air surfaces. Keep skin clean and dry, since moisture from sweat, urine or wound fluid macerates skin and lowers its tolerance to pressure. Maintain adequate protein and hydration, because a malnourished person builds new tissue poorly. A Stage 3 or 4 injury can take months to close and genuinely kills people through osteomyelitis and sepsis.

Diabetic foot ulcers combine three deficits that reinforce one another. Years of elevated glucose damage peripheral nerves from the toes upward, so protective sensation fails and a stone in a shoe, a blister or a scald goes entirely unfelt. The same disease narrows small and large arteries, so the injured tissue has poor blood supply with which to heal. And elevated glucose impairs neutrophil function, blunting the response to bacteria. The practical consequence is that daily foot inspection, including between the toes and using a mirror for the soles, is the main defence rather than fussiness, and any diabetic foot wound deserves prompt professional assessment however unremarkable it appears.

sections.heading: Scarring and long-term wound outcomes
sections.body:
Any injury breaching the dermis heals with a scar, because mammalian repair is a patch rather than a regeneration. Undamaged dermis is a basket-weave of collagen fibres running in many directions, which is what gives skin strength and pliability in every direction at once. Repair lays down type III collagen quickly in parallel bundles aligned with tension, then converts it over months into stronger type I collagen — but the parallel arrangement is never undone.
